Republican midterm convention 2026: What to know about Trump’s Dallas event
Unorthodox event seeks to mobilise midterm Republican voters, even as Trump approval rating tanks.
The United States Republican Party – and its talisman President Donald Trump – is descending on Dallas, Texas, to host a rare convention before the midterm elections in November.
Usually reserved for presidential election cycles, Trump’s call to hold the high-cost event before the November 3 midterm vote has underscored both the president’s unorthodox campaign style and the urgency of the political moment for his Republican Party.

Trump’s approval rating has tanked in the lead-up to the midterm vote, with polls pointing to a panoply of factors, most notably the US-Israel war on Iran and its knock-on economic effects for US consumers.
The lack of enthusiasm threatens what are already considered long-shot odds in the Republicans’ effort to hold on to control of the House of Representatives. Shifting public opinion has also put control of the Senate increasingly in play, although Democrats still face an uphill battle to pull off an upset.
A loss of control in either chamber would serve as a major check on Trump’s authority in the final two years of his second term.
But not all Republicans have bought into Trump and the party’s claims that the convention will spur voter turnout.
Several, particularly those in the tightest races, have kept the event at arm’s length amid concerns that associating with the president could only further mobilise his detractors.
Here’s what to know:
When and where is the Republican midterm convention?
The convention will be hosted at the American Airlines Center in Dallas, Texas, on Wednesday, September 9 and Thursday, September 10.
The event is expected to run from 3pm to 9pm Central Time (20:00 to 02:00 GMT) on both days.
Trump is scheduled to speak on both nights, including a Wednesday address and the convention’s closing keynote on Thursday from 8pm to 9pm Central Time (01:00 to 02:00 GMT on Friday).
US Vice President JD Vance will close out night one with a speech.

corpus.title: Welcome to Trumpapalooza, the unusual convention Republicans hope will save the midterm elections
corpus.signal_text:
Welcome to Trumpapalooza, the unusual convention Republicans hope will save the midterm elections
Dozens of candidates in tight districts have skipped the MAGA conclave convened to glorify Donald Trump, fearing the toxic influence of the president
Donald Trump announced in June that he would hold “a truly historic event.” The hyperbole is typical for him, but the timing is unusual: a Republican Party convention in Dallas, Texas, less than two months before the midterm elections.
The Trump rendezvous with history takes place on September 9 and 10. And it is true that it is unprecedented. It is being billed like the kind of conclave both parties stage every four years, shortly before presidential elections, to pick their nominees and display coalition unity — but this time it promises to be more of a damage-control operation: polls ahead of November 3 favor the Democrats. All seats in the House and one-third of the Senate are at stake, and it is possible the Republicans could lose control of one or both chambers — and with it, the legislative initiative.
The gathering already has an informal name: Trumpapalooza. It is nicknamed after a famous rock festival, Lollapalooza, but also as a clear signal: like almost everything happening in the Republican Party since his return to power, what takes place over the next two days at the American Airlines Stadium in Dallas will revolve around Trump.
The difference is that the 50,000 people who traveled from across the country to attend the Republican convention in Milwaukee a couple of years ago — held a few days after the then-candidate survived an assassination attempt at an outdoor rally — arrived with more enthusiasm than the 20,000 attendees the organizers say they expect in Dallas. But the menus will look similar: a diet of America First candidate speeches, all the MAGA pageantry and excess, a playlist of the leader’s favorite songs — including one in particular, Lee Greenwood’s God Bless the U.S.A. — and not one but two Trump rallies, which will be “like no other,” he promised in June.
Two nights in a row
Scheduling the main act for two consecutive nights was the organizers’ gambit to prevent interest from flagging among attendees, who were asked to consider a $25,000 donation to participate.
